guide.title: Trauma Systems & Kinematics
guide.lead: Read the wreck before you read the patient. Energy rises with the square of speed, and each crash is really three collisions. The mechanism tells you which hidden injuries to hunt for, and the field triage criteria tell you where to take the patient.

sections.title: Mechanism → suspect
rows: Head and neck, chest (steering wheel), liver and spleen, aorta
Ears and lungs (pressure), fragments, being thrown, burns
notes: Kinetic energy = ½ × mass × velocity²: doubling speed gives 4 times the energy.

groups.title: Injuries
items: Penetrating injury to head, neck, torso or proximal limbs
Skull deformity; chest wall instability; suspected pelvic fracture
2 or more proximal long-bone fractures; crushed, mangled or pulseless limb; amputation above the wrist or ankle
Bleeding needing a tourniquet or packing; spinal injury with new weakness

groups.title: Physiology
items: Unable to follow commands (motor GCS below 6)
Respiratory rate below 10 or above 29/min, or SpO₂ below 90%
Systolic below 90 mmHg or heart rate greater than systolic BP
Age 65 or older with systolic below 110 mmHg

groups.title: Mechanism
items: Fall over 10 feet (3 m), any age
Ejection, major intrusion, death in the same compartment
Pedestrian or cyclist struck at over 20 mph; rider thrown

groups.title: Patient
items: Age 65 or older, anticoagulants, pregnancy over 20 weeks

quiz.q: High-speed side impact on the driver's side, left upper quadrant and hip pain. Highest-risk organ?
quiz.explanation: Left-sided impact loads the spleen and left ribs.

quiz.q: Which finding alone sends an adult to the highest-level trauma centre (Field Triage 2021)?
quiz.explanation: Also respiratory rate below 10 or above 29/min, SpO₂ below 90%, or unable to follow commands.

quiz.q: Unrestrained driver, bent steering wheel, wheel-shaped chest bruise, stable vital signs. Highest suspicion?
options: Cardiac and pulmonary contusion (and aortic injury)

quiz.q: An alert adult fell 25 feet with no visible injury and stable vital signs. Destination?
options: Trauma centre: falls over 10 feet (3 m) are a moderate-risk mechanism
quiz.explanation: Field Triage 2021 uses over 10 feet for all ages.

quiz.q: Doubling vehicle speed multiplies crash energy by:
quiz.explanation: Energy rises with the square of velocity.

options: Child pedestrians: femur, chest/abdomen and head injuries
quiz.explanation: Children are hit higher on the body than adults.

quiz.q: A lap-belt-only restraint is linked to:
Which is a moderate-risk (yellow) patient factor?
quiz.explanation: Also age 65 or older and pregnancy over 20 weeks.

quiz.q: The third collision in a crash is:
options: Organs hitting the inside of the body
quiz.explanation: Brain against skull, aorta tearing, liver and spleen tearing.

flashcards.question: Trauma centre levels
flashcards.answer: Level I: comprehensive, research and teaching. II: comprehensive care. III: resuscitate and stabilise. IV: stabilise in remote areas. Other countries use major trauma centres and units.

flashcards.question: Field triage 2021
flashcards.answer: High-risk (red): injury patterns and physiology. Moderate-risk (yellow): mechanism and patient factors. Plus EMS judgement.

flashcards.question: Three collisions
flashcards.answer: Vehicle hits object; body hits vehicle; organs hit the inside of the body.

flashcards.question: Why speed matters
flashcards.answer: Kinetic energy = ½ × mass × velocity²: doubling speed gives 4 times the energy.

flashcards.question: Frontal crash patterns
flashcards.answer: Up-and-over: head, chest, abdomen. Down-and-under: knees, femurs, hips.

flashcards.question: Blunt vs penetrating
flashcards.answer: Blunt spreads energy widely (hidden injuries); penetrating concentrates it along the track (small wound, deep damage).

flashcards.question: Blast injury phases
flashcards.answer: Primary (pressure), secondary (fragments), tertiary (thrown), quaternary (burns, crush, inhalation), quinary (later effects).

flashcards.question: Waddell's triad
flashcards.answer: Child pedestrian: femur fracture, chest or abdominal injury, head injury.

critical.scenario: An unrestrained driver hit a barrier at about 90 km/h with severe intrusion. Wheel-shaped chest bruise. BP 106/74, HR 116, RR 26, SpO₂ 93%. Reduced breath sounds on the left, crackles on the right.
critical.question: What do you suspect, and the transport priority?

options.t: Cardiac and pulmonary contusion, hemo- or pneumothorax, possible aortic injury: oxygen to target, rapid assessment, trauma centre

options.f: The mechanism and findings say otherwise.
Hypoxia and abnormal breath sounds are injury.

options.t: Full secondary survey on scene first

critical.explanation: Aortic injury can look stable until it ruptures.
critical.kpi: Uses mechanism of injury to anticipate thoracic injuries and destination

critical.scenario: A man fell 25 feet onto his feet. Severe low back pain, both heels painful, weak legs (3/5), sensation intact. BP 118/74, HR 104.
critical.question: Injury pattern?

options.t: Axial load: both heels, possible lumbar burst fracture and cord injury – spinal motion restriction, trauma centre

options.f: Weak legs mean the spine is involved.

options.t: Walk him to the ambulance to test

critical.explanation: Falls over 10 feet (3 m) are a moderate-risk mechanism; new weakness makes it high-risk.
critical.kpi: Recognizes axial loading injury patterns and spinal involvement

critical.scenario: A 7-year-old (22 kg) was hit by a car: deformed right thigh, left chest bruise, chin cut, holding his abdomen. BP 98/62, HR 130.
critical.question: Pattern and plan?

options.t: Waddell's triad (femur, chest/abdomen, head): rapid assessment, splint, pediatric trauma centre
Femur only: splint and closest hospital
options.f: Look for the other two injuries.

options.t: Minor injuries: parents can drive him

critical.explanation: A femur fracture alone can lose a lot of blood in a child.
critical.kpi: Recognizes Waddell's triad and selects a pediatric trauma centre
